title: Vinayaka Chaturthi in Tamil Nadu: fervour, creative pandals and colossal offerings mark festival
excerpt: From Madurai's colossal Mukkuruni Kozhukattai to a 25-kg offering atop Tiruchirappalli's Rockfort, Tamil Nadu celebrated Vinayaka Chaturthi with devotion and spectacle as police cleared 36,000 idols statewide.
body:
• Tamil Nadu celebrated Vinayaka Chaturthi on September 14 with temple rituals, creative neighbourhood pandals and massive traditional offerings across the state.
  • Madurai's Sri Meenakshi Sundareshwar Temple offered a colossal 'Mukkuruni Kozhukattai' to its 7-foot monolithic Mukkuruni Vinayakar, while a five-year-old elephant named Durga made her festive debut.
  • Thousands climbed the 417 steps to Tiruchirappalli's Ucchi Pillayar Temple atop the Rockfort, where a 25-kg kozhukattai opened the shrine's 14-day Peruvizha festival.
  • Tamil Nadu Police cleared the installation of 36,000 Ganesh idols statewide; 16,500 personnel and 500 Home Guards were deployed in Chennai, with immersions scheduled for September 19-20.

Vinayaka Chaturthi was celebrated across Tamil Nadu on September 14 with religious fervour, creative displays and colossal offerings, as temples drew thousands of devotees and neighbourhood pandals unveiled imaginative idols, according to The Hindu.

Context & Background

At the Narthana Vinayagar shrine, the idol was anointed with holy water, milk, sandalwood and honey before being dressed in a glittering gold kavacham (armour), drawing thousands to the flower-lined Mada streets. In Madurai, the spotlight fell on the 7-foot monolithic Mukkuruni Vinayakar inside the Sri Meenakshi Sundareshwar Temple. Continuing a centuries-old tradition, priests prepared a single massive 'Mukkuruni Kozhukattai' — a sweet rice-flour dumpling — as the offering. Devotees and priests also welcomed Durga, a five-year-old elephant recently relocated from Assam, who made her festive debut with a flower-showering ceremony; the temple already cares for an older resident elephant, Parvathi.

https://x.com/ANI/status/2099129752149741605

In Tiruchirappalli, thousands climbed 417 steep steps to the 7th-century Ucchi Pillayar Temple atop the 273-foot Rockfort, where the hill-top shrine launched its 14-day Peruvizha festival by offering a 25-kg kozhukattai. In Chennai, pandals across Triplicane, Mylapore and other neighbourhoods blended devotion with local pop culture, unveiling idols themed on mythological epics and cinema characters.

At Puliakulam in Coimbatore, special poojas and alankaras marked the festival at the Sri Arulmigu Mundhi Vinayagar temple, home to a 190-tonne monolithic granite idol — 19 feet 10 inches high and 11 feet 10 inches wide. The deity was decorated with 50 kg of sandalwood paste. At Eral in Tuticorin district, devotees erected a replica of the Tirupparankundram deepathoon (stone pillar) with Ganesh lighting the lamp, expressing their wish to light the Karthigai deepam atop the ancient pillar. A temple elephant joined the procession at Rameswaram.

Impact & Analysis

The scale of the celebrations is matched by the machinery behind them. Tamil Nadu Police granted permission for the installation of 36,000 Ganesh idols at public places across the state after organisers met conditions laid down by the Madras High Court, the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board, the Fire and Rescue Services Department, local bodies and the police, IANS reported. In Chennai alone, city police permitted 1,562 idols at approved locations.

Security arrangements are extensive: 16,500 police personnel and 500 Home Guards were deployed across the Chennai police jurisdiction. Organisers were instructed to install CCTV cameras at public worship sites, deploy volunteers to guard idols and regulate crowds, comply with rules on idol size and materials, and follow fire safety, electrical safety, environmental and traffic norms. Processions and immersions are scheduled for September 19 and 20, along routes approved in advance, with organisers required to complete immersion within the stipulated time.

Diaspora Angle

Vinayaka Chaturthi is among the most widely observed festivals for Tamil communities around the world, and celebrations in Tamil Nadu set the cultural template — from the 190-tonne granite Vinayagar of Puliakulam to the centuries-old Mukkuruni traditions of Madurai — that diaspora temples and associations recreate abroad.

What's Next

Public celebrations continue through the immersion processions on September 19 and 20, while the Ucchi Pillayar Temple's 14-day Peruvizha runs its course. Police will maintain surveillance along procession routes and immersion points until the last idol is immersed.
